stemBlocks.value: Quadrilateral O has vertices (1, 1), (2, 3), (4, 1) and (3, 0). Quadrilateral M has vertices (1, 3), (3, 7), (7, 3) and (5, 1), and quadrilateral N has vertices (-1, -1), (-2, -3), (-4, -1) and (-3, 0). M and N are the images of O under two different transformations; describe each of those single transformations fully.
Think first: Check the sizes first: if the image is bigger it must be an enlargement, and if it is the same size but turned round, look for a rotation.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p265-q12 from workbook page 265.

solutionSteps.instruction: Read the vertices of the three quadrilaterals from the grid and pair them up.

contentBlocks.value: Result: Three sets of four vertices

solutionSteps.instruction: Compare a side of O with the matching side of M.

contentBlocks.value: In O the step from (1, 1) to (2, 3) is (1, 2); in M the step from (1, 3) to (3, 7) is (2, 4), which is twice as long. Every side of M is twice the matching side of O.

solutionSteps.instruction: Find the centre of the enlargement using centre = 2 x object - image.
Now compare O with N vertex by vertex.
Name the transformation with that rule.

contentBlocks.value: Changing the sign of both coordinates turns every point through a half turn about the origin; for a half turn the direction of turning does not need to be stated.
Result: Rotation of 180 degrees about the origin (0, 0)

strategyBlocks.value: Match corresponding vertices of O with those of M and N. For M compare side lengths to get a scale factor and then solve for the centre; for N spot the coordinate rule and name the rotation.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: O onto M: an enlargement with centre (1, -1) and scale factor 2.  O onto N: a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin (0, 0).

whyThisWorks.value: An enlargement multiplies every displacement from a fixed centre by the scale factor, so lengths double while angles stay the same and the image is similar to the object. A rotation of 180 degrees about the origin sends the position vector v to -v, which is exactly the rule (x, y) -> (-x, -y); it preserves both size and orientation, so N is congruent to O and not a mirror image of it.

commonErrors.misconception: Describing O onto N as a reflection, since a half turn also looks 'flipped' at a glance but preserves orientation.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Describing O onto N as a reflection, since a half turn also looks 'flipped' at a glance but preserves orientation.

commonErrors.misconception: Giving the enlargement without its centre.

examTip.value: For a half turn, test the rule (x, y) -> (-x, -y) on every vertex. If it works for all of them the centre is the origin; if not, the centre is elsewhere and you must find it.
